items.title: 53279_Lee Young Oral History Interview
items.q: he made many, many records with Lady Day and Teddy Wilson

ctx.x: Well, that was the first time I really knew that was Lester playing on Basie's records. So he -- his style, I can't say about that; I don't know where he came up with it, because I was not around, you know, during that time, but

when he came to us, and joined the small group that I had, he was well established, he was well known, he made many, many records with Lady Day and Teddy Wilson, and he did a couple of things with Benny Goodman. Was it "Tippy Tippy Tin?" No, that was something else -- but he made something with Benny Goodman that was kind of a classic; it was -- he played a good solo on it, but you know, when he first came out here, you know how the West Coast and the East Coast was? I don't know if you were aware of that.

But the East Coast musicians -- they didn't know too much of what was happening on the West Coast, you know? And maybe it was because of the trains or the covered wagons or whatever we had at that time. But Bumps -- everyone felt as though Bumps Myers, the people here in town, which was the tenor player, would really blow Lester away, because they always had their favorites, but it took them about a couple of sessions to understand what he was about. Because he really came up with jamming, you know, in New York,…
